sceneHappening: What a church needs in its leaders, and the church itself as the household of the living God
summary: "This is a faithful saying: someone who seeks to be an overseer desires a good work." The overseer "must be without reproach, the husband of one wife, temperate, sensible, modest, hospitable, good at teaching; not a drinker, not violent, not greedy for money, but gentle, not quarrelsome, not covetous; one who rules his own house well, having children in subjection with all reverence (but how could someone who doesn't know how to rule one's own house take care of God's assembly?); not a new convert, lest being puffed up he fall into the same condemnation as the devil. Moreover he must have good testimony from those who are outside, to avoid falling into reproach and the snare of the devil." "Servants" (the Greek word is diakonos, "deacons") must likewise be "reverent, not double-tongued, not addicted to much wine, not greedy for money, holding the mystery of the faith in a pure conscience." They are to be tested first, "then let them serve if they are blameless." Verse 11 says "Their wives in the same way must be reverent, not slanderers, temperate, and faithful in all things," and verse 12 repeats that these servants are to be "husbands of one wife, ruling their children and their own houses well." Those who serve well "gain for themselves a good standing, and great boldness in the faith which is in Christ Jesus." Paul writes hoping to come soon, "but if I wait long, that you may know how men ought to behave themselves in God's house, which is the assembly of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth." The chapter ends with a short poem: "Without controversy, the mystery of godliness is great: God was revealed in the flesh, justified in the spirit, seen by angels, preached among the nations, believed on in the world, and received up in glory."
whySettingMatters: Churches in the first century met in homes, and the household was the model for how they were ordered; that is why the first test for a leader is how he runs his own house (3:4-5), and why the church is called "God's house" (3:15). The word "overseer" (episkopos) was in ordinary use for a supervisor, and in Acts 20:17 and 20:28 and in Titus 1:5-7 Paul seems to use it interchangeably with "elder" (presbyteros); later the church used it for a single bishop over many congregations. The qualities listed are mostly ordinary virtues that people in Ephesus would have admired in any leader, with one gift added: being "able to teach," which is the answer to the false teachers of chapter 1. Several phrases are debated. "Husband of one wife" (literally "a one-woman man") has been read as forbidding polygamy, forbidding remarriage after a spouse's death or divorce, requiring married leaders, or requiring faithfulness in marriage; the Greek does not settle it. In 3:11 "their wives in the same way" could also be translated "the women" and may refer to women who serve as deacons, as Phoebe is called a "servant" (diakonos) of the assembly at Cenchreae in Romans 16:1. The poem in 3:16 looks like an early hymn or creed. It runs in pairs, from earth to heaven and back (flesh and spirit, angels and nations, world and glory), and its opening word is "who" in many manuscripts and "God" in others, so the translation "God was revealed" is not the only reading. "Pillar" is an image from building; Ephesus was famous for the great columns of its temple of Artemis, which may lie behind the picture.

questions: Most of the overseer's qualities are about character rather than skill. What does that suggest about what a church most needs from its leaders?
"Husband of one wife" and "their wives" (or "the women") in 3:2 and 3:11 are read in different ways. What do you think is at stake in each reading?
Paul calls the church "the pillar and ground of the truth." How does that fit with the idea that it must also be guarded and corrected?
The poem in 3:16 moves from "revealed in the flesh" to "received up in glory." What do you notice about what it chooses to include?

"The overseer therefore must be without reproach" (3:1-2).
"The husband of one wife" (3:2, 3:12) and "their wives" or "the women" (3:11).
"One who rules his own house well" (3:4-5, 3:12).
"The same condemnation as the devil" (3:6) and "the snare of the devil" (3:7).
"Servants, in the same way, must be reverent" (3:8, 3:12).
"Not double-tongued" (3:8). The word appears only here.
"Holding the mystery of the faith" (3:9) and "the mystery of godliness" (3:16).
"A good standing" (3:13). The word appears only here.
"How men ought to behave themselves in God's house" (3:15).
"God's assembly" (3:5) and "the assembly of the living God" (3:15).
"The pillar and ground of the truth" (3:15). The word appears only here.
"Without controversy" (3:16). The word appears only here.
"Justified in the spirit" (3:16) and "the Spirit says expressly" (4:1).
